# ADR-0078: A Kueue workload's result files leave the pod on an injected sidecar's log

> **Status:** proposed | **Date:** 2026-11-21

**References:** [RFC-0002:C-TASK-FILES](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-task-files), [ADR-0068](../adr/ADR-0068.md), [ADR-0075](../adr/ADR-0075.md)

## Context

<<<<<<< HEAD
A run submits a Job through crucible-kueue and the Job writes files: benchmark results, a profile, a report. A task can declare files as output ([RFC-0002:C-TASK-FILES](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-task-files)), but only files in its own workspace, and nothing carries a file from the Job's pod to that workspace.

The one channel out of a pod today is `workload_logs`: text, at most 1 MiB, returned as a tool result. An agent that wants files has the Job print a base64 archive and reads it back in pieces, so every byte passes through the model.

Constraints:

- The server's service account reads pods, pod logs and events in a workload namespace. It cannot exec into a pod and it keeps no state.
- The caller picks the workload's image and command. Anything mounted into the pod is within their reach, and the image may hold no archive tool.
- A pod that stays up to be read holds its Kueue quota, GPUs included.
- Results are wanted most when the Job fails partway.
- A file declared as task output is small: one run's declared files total at most 256 MiB.
- The manifest allowlist already admits an `emptyDir` and an init container with `restartPolicy: Always` (a native sidecar, Kubernetes 1.29 and later). The kubelet sends such a sidecar SIGTERM once the pod's regular containers have exited, pass or fail, and its exit code does not change the pod's phase or the Job's.
- The kubelet rotates the log of a running container only. A container that writes and exits leaves its whole log readable until the pod is deleted.


## Decision

`workload_plan` and `workload_submit` take `results`, a directory in the workload's container. The server adds an `emptyDir` mounted there and a native sidecar that mounts it read-only. When the main container exits the sidecar writes one archive of the directory to its own stdout, with a list of the files, their sizes and a digest, and exits. `workload_results` reads that container's log with the access `workload_logs` already needs and answers the list. Asked for file contents, it checks the digest and answers them within a byte budget.

- The sidecar is the server's own image run as a collector, so a cluster mirrors no second image.
- The added volume and container are part of the plan hash and are reported with the server's other changes to the manifest.
- The archive is bounded by a server setting, and the list by a fixed number of files. Past either the sidecar writes the list and sizes and no contents.
- The sidecar runs as the main container's `runAsUser` when the manifest sets one.
- The client library writes the files to a directory, refusing a path that leaves it. A command or evaluate task then declares them like any other file in its workspace.
- `results` is taken for a Job. A kind that serves until stopped is refused.

The log is the transport because the server can already read it and the node already keeps it: no new grant, no storage, no route from workload pods to the server, and no credential in a pod the caller controls.


## Consequences

A Job's files reach a task's workspace without passing through a model, from an image that knows nothing about crucible, and from a Job that failed as well as one that passed.

The server stays stateless. Any replica answers `workload_results`, and a restart loses nothing.

Results live as long as the pod. Past `finished_retention_seconds`, or after `workload_stop` deletes the pods, they are gone, so a caller collects before then.

The archive is base64 in a container log, a third larger than the files, and a cluster's log pipeline ingests it. The bound keeps that to megabytes. A larger artifact is pushed to a registry and passed on by its location, which [RFC-0002:C-TASK-FILES](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-task-files) already asks of anything that outlives its run.

The sidecar's requests add to the pod's, so the plan's fit and the quota charged include them.

A file the sidecar's user cannot read is listed as unread, not dropped. Where a namespace assigns one UID to every container of a pod this does not arise; elsewhere a manifest that sets no `runAsUser` and writes owner-only files gets a list of unread files.

A sidecar that fails does not fail the Job. `workload_results` says no archive was written, and why when the log shows it.

An agent's own shell still cannot fetch the files: the sandbox carries the token only on the harness's requests ([ADR-0068](../adr/ADR-0068.md)). An agent sees the list and small files through the tool; a pack that wants the files as task output collects them in a command task ([ADR-0075](../adr/ADR-0075.md)). A results client among the sandbox binaries the token grant covers would let an agent write them to its workspace, and is not decided here.

A Job with several pods has one archive per pod. A RayJob, JobSet or PyTorchJob has several pod templates, and which of them collect is not decided here.

A cluster older than Kubernetes 1.29 has no native sidecars, and `results` is refused there.


## Alternatives Considered

### An injected native sidecar writes an archive of the directory to its own log; the server reads the log (accepted)
=======
An engine deployed on a cluster we manage is trusted with model credentials because we control the cluster. We do not control an external cluster. An operator there, or anyone who takes a pod, holds whatever the deployment carries. Today that includes provider keys. The controller resolves providers for every pod and hands the engine the inference document with their keys ([ADR-0065](../adr/ADR-0065.md)), and the engine copies agent-visible secrets into the agent sandboxes.

An external cluster is still a useful place to run the parts of a playbook that need no model: builds, tests, measures, reports. A run with no agent binding already calls its model with whatever credentials the environment carries ([RFC-0001:C-INFERENCE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-inference)), so the engine there must be unable to call a model at all, whatever its environment carries and whatever a pack asks for. Provider keys are not the only credentials a dispatch delivers. The run's own token, the git sidecar's GitHub credential, and per-task tokens for the run's servers arrive with it. The engine must hold none of them.

## Decision

We turn the engine's model features off at compile time. A cargo feature `agents`, on by default, compiles them in: agent turns, model-decided routes, and the `[agent]` configuration that reads and passes credentials. The external-cluster build omits the feature and is the **hard-tools-only engine**, built with `cargo build -p crucible --no-default-features --features hard-tools-only`. The `hard-tools-only` feature is empty. It only names the build.

The hard-tools-only engine refuses every plan task that asks a model: an agent turn, a model-decided route ([RFC-0001:C-ROUTE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-route)), and the scored loop's propose turn. These are the tasks `TaskKind::spends` marks for the cost ceiling. `crucible plan run` refuses the plan before dispatch, with an error naming the task and the kinds that still run. `crucible check` reports each such task as a finding, so a pack this build cannot run does not pass check on it. The task runner refuses the same tasks again, so no caller of this build can execute one outside `plan run` either. The mechanism is the one [RFC-0002:C-PLAYBOOK-CAPS](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-playbook-caps) already defines, where a capability the substrate does not have truncates the plan before any spend. Here the capability is absent by build rather than by dispatch.

The build also removes every credential the engine could hold. It reads no inference document, so no run of this build can reach a decision model. It applies no `[agent]` table, so no harness pinning, skills toolbox, `[agent].env` or secret relay, or `[mcp]` server is configured. `--agent-cmd`, `--harness`, and `--model` are refused. A remote server the controller grants is refused at run start, naming the grant, since its tokens are credentials this build holds nowhere. The local socket servers are hard tools and run: buildit and crucible-git serve the run itself over a unix socket with no token. A pack naming `[workflow].servers` is still refused before any work, since those take task tokens. No decision desk opens, so a required human-decided route truncates the plan and an advisory one is skipped with its dependents. `--rerun-of` must name a local state directory, not a run's evidence on the controller. No S3 code is compiled in at all (`hard-tools-only` carries no `publish`): no `fetch`, no run publishing, no AWS SDK, so an ambient cloud credential has no code that reads it.

The run's record still reaches the controller, without credentials. A controller that runs open already answers every caller as its dev identity, and it accepts a run's evidence the same way, with no bearer. The full record of session, declared files, and git memory is stored there, and a rerun reads it back the same way. A guarded controller still requires the run's own token, which this build never reads. There the tokenless upload is refused, the run marks its session undelivered, and the controller scrapes the session from the pod's log. A guarded controller's evidence route is unchanged.

Command, evaluate, and report tasks, and output-decided routes, run as before. The refusal is at plan admission, not in the compiler. The library stays feature-free, so a controller links the same library and validates every pack, whatever build its images run.

## Consequences

- The library, the workflow compiler, and the controller are unchanged. Only the binary's behavior differs per build, and the default build behaves exactly as before.
- The agent modules stay compiled in the hard-tools-only binary because the reporter, control, and openshell layers share their event types, but no path reaches them. Admission, check, and the runner all refuse first, and no credential the environment carries is read. Tests that exercise agent behavior are gated to the `agents` build, and CI clippies and tests the stripped feature set so it cannot break unnoticed.
- A run's record reaches the controller with no credential on either side. On an open controller the full evidence (session, declared files, git memory) is uploaded without a token, and a rerun reads it back without one. On a guarded controller the tokenless upload is refused, the session is marked undelivered, and the pod-log scrape recovers the record. The scrape recovers the session only, so a scraped run's files and commits stay in the pod. The open acceptance adds no authority, because an open controller already admits every caller as its dev identity on every other route, and a guarded controller's route still requires the run token. A launch dispatched to such a target by today's controller would deliver the inference document, the run's servers, and the pod token. The engine never reads the token and refuses the rest at admission. Dispatch-side policy (resolve no models, deliver no run secrets or servers to such a target) remains a follow-up. It would make the pod cleaner, not safer, because the engine already refuses or ignores what is delivered.
- A pack with agent tasks or a required human decision fails on a hard-tools-only engine at plan load, minutes later than an API-side refusal would, and it spends nothing. Its author gets the task name and the kinds that run instead.
- Dropping `publish` from the build also drops the bin's `required-features` field. The binary now compiles with no features at all, and `--no-default-features --features hard-tools-only` is the documented form of the stripped build.
- The image build carries the feature set as a build-arg (`ENGINE_FEATURES` on the self-contained runtime Containerfile), so the external-cluster image differs from the standard one by that one argument.

## Alternatives Considered

### A default-on `agents` feature, omitted by the external-cluster build, which refuses model-asking tasks at admission, check, and the runner, and holds no credential (accepted)

### The server copies the files out of the pod with exec (rejected)

- **Pros:** No sidecar and no change to the manifest
- **Cons:** The server's service account gains pods/exec in every workload namespace, The pod has to stay up to be read, holding its quota, The image needs tar
- **Rejected because:** Exec on every workload pod is a far wider grant than reading logs, and a waiting pod holds GPUs.

### The workload writes to a PersistentVolumeClaim that is read afterwards (rejected)

- **Pros:** No size limit, Results outlive the pod
- **Cons:** The strict allowlist refuses volume claims, Reading the claim takes another pod in the namespace, Claims have to be created, sized and deleted per workload
- **Rejected because:** It needs a second pod and a claim lifecycle to move a few files.

### Leave it to the workload: print an archive to its own log and read it with workload_logs (rejected)

- **Pros:** No server change
- **Cons:** Every image needs an archive tool and a script that runs on failure too, The archive is interleaved with the program's output and capped at 1 MiB, An agent reads it through the model
- **Rejected because:** It is the workaround this replaces.
